https://www.naftemporiki.gr/english/2139.text: Αγορές Χρηματιστήριο Ταμπλό ΧΑ Real Time Παράγωγα Αμοιβαία κεφάλαια Ομόλογα Κύπρος Ξένοι Δείκτες Ισοτιμιίες Μέταλλα Excel Utilities Metastock Τεχνική Ανάλυση Hellenic Defence Systems targets stronger performance; 40 mln euro revenue English Hellenic Defence Systems targets stronger performance; 40 mln euro revenue Δευτέρα, 20 Ιουλίου 2026 11:36 The company, Greece's main domestic manufacturer of weapons systems and ammunition for the armed forces, is targeting revenue of 40 million euros in 2026, up from 14.08 million euros in 2025 Share: Share via Facebook Share via Twitter Share via LinkedIn Share via Email Share via WhatsApp Copy Link Προσθέστε την «Ν» ως προτιμώμενη πηγή στο Google Hellenic Defence Systems (HDS) expects a significant improvement in its financial performance from 2026, supported by expanded production capacity that is expected to drive higher sales of defence products and services. The company, Greece’s main domestic manufacturer of weapons systems and ammunition for the armed forces, is targeting revenue of 40 million euros in 2026, up from 14.08 million euros in 2025. It also expects to return to marginal profitability after posting a net loss of 2.2 million euros in 2025, compared with a loss of 25.01 million euros in 2024. HDS reported a positive gross profit of 11.8 million euros in 2025, reflecting improved production performance. Shareholders’ equity and working capital also turned positive for the first time since the company’s establishment. Outstanding loans stood at 73.1 million euros as of Dec. 31, 2025. New strategy aims for financial self-sufficiency According to sources, HDS’s management has prepared a new strategic and business plan, which is expected to be presented at an extraordinary general meeting scheduled for late July 2026. The plan aims to make the company financially self-sufficient within the next three years, eliminating the need for recurring state financial support. The previous business plan was drafted about 15 years ago. In its 2025 financial report, management said the company’s financial position remains challenging despite improved operating performance and continued government backing. The company received a 32 million euro capital injection in 2025 and a further 49.8 million euros in equity funding so far in 2026. Expansion backed by EU funding and international partnerships Under the European Union’s ASAP (Act in Support of Ammunition Production) programme, HDS has secured funding to build two explosives production facilities. Earlier this year, the company signed an agreement with Czech defence group CSG, through its subsidiary MSM Greece, to establish the Hellenic Ammunition joint venture in Lavrio. The venture will manufacture large-calibre ammunition in Greece. For 2026, HDS is focusing on further expanding production capacity, securing long-term defence manufacturing contracts through international industrial partnerships, and continuing its financial restructuring to strengthen the company’s long-term sustainability and growth prospects. The company also plans to complete the legal liquidation of inactive subsidiaries during 2026, while management is evaluating opportunities to further develop and monetize HDS’s real estate assets. Photograph: ©Tudor Panduru View image in fullscreen Problematic … Fjord, written and directed by Cristian Mungiu. Photograph: ©Tudor Panduru Movies Dogmatic Nordic liberals v eastern family values: culture-clash drama Fjord touches nerves in Norway and Romania Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner echoes the news story of a Romanian couple whose children were taken by the Norwegian government. As it heads to London film festival, two writers explain how the film exposes real hypocrisies Andrei Popoviciu and Magnus Nome Fri 16 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 02.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google ‘On paper, both countries agree that smacking your child is illegal’: Romanian journalist Andrei Popoviciu When Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord was shown in Romania as a one-day preview this June, the reception was extraordinary. Across 53 towns and 96 cinemas, the film reportedly pulled in over 40,000 viewers in a single night, a number arthouse cinema rarely sees in Romania. But the response here had little to do with cinema. It felt instead like a reopening of a familiar fault line about the clash of values within the EU itself. Fjord review - Cristian Mungiu at sea with strange child abuse drama starring Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan Read more The film echoes events from 2015, when the five children of Marius and Ruth Bodnariu, a Pentecostal couple from Romania living in Norway – part of a Neo-Protestant minority long viewed with suspicion in Orthodox Romania – were removed from their home by Barnevernet, Norway’s child welfare authority, amid concerns over possible corporal punishment and religious indoctrination. The fallout in Romania stretched on for months, with diplomatic friction, public demonstrations and constant media coverage. The children were eventually returned, and the Bodnarius later resettled in Romania. Mungiu doesn’t retell the story beat for beat, but Romanian viewers had no trouble recognising where it came from. What divided viewers here was what the film did with a well-known story. Some have called it “dangerously confusing”, raising questions about abuse, integration and belief without taking a clear position. Others counter that its stance is embedded in form, in how sympathy is distributed, which characters get interiority and which are reduced to function. To some, it’s a brave critique of dogmatic liberalism, while to others, it dilutes a clear moral boundary on corporal punishment while extending undue warmth to religious conservatism. At its most charged, the debate spills into a broader anxiety about whether the EU can sustain its own contradictions. That tension surfaced again weeks later, when a viral video of a Romanian mother mistreating her daughter in public reignited the same split online (many defended her as exercising necessary discipline, others condemned her outright) suggesting attitudes here may be shifting, but unevenly. It’s worth pausing on how narrow the legal gap between the two countries actually is, because the film’s reception treats it as a chasm. Romania criminalised corporal punishment in 2004, Norway in 1987. On paper, both already agree smacking your child is illegal, but the real distance is between law and belief. A UN human rights body recently noted that despite the ban, Romania still needs to shift the mindset of parents who believe corporal punishment works better than the alternative. The Orthodox church, meanwhile, has never fully shed a folk theology in which strict discipline raises a righteous child, even as doctrine and law increasingly say otherwise. What’s notable is how little agreement there is about what the film actually endorses. Some say the supporting characters – social workers, lawyers, neighbours – are too thin to carry the moral weight asked of them. Others accuse Mungiu of stacking the deck, giving the Christian-conservative family warmth while leaving Norwegian institutions cold and procedural. Mungiu has spoken of challenging “leftwing fundamentalism”, a phrase conservatives have seized on as vindication, though he has equally condemned its rightwing counterpart. Defenders counter that a director sympathetic to victims must be willing to defend a conservative minority in a progressive society just as he’d defend a progressive one surrounded by conservatives, since majorities of any stripe tend to need an “other” to demonise. Some critics have said that intent stops mattering once a film reaches an audience, so whatever Mungiu meant by refusing to pick a side, the dramatic architecture produces sympathy for the family almost by default. My own sense is that Fjord is a film about whether a system convinced of its own good intentions can imagine being wrong. It’s the same reflex found in churches, homes and government offices from Oslo to Bucharest and across the polarised world we live in – the certainty that one’s side only ever needs vindication, never correction. ‘Norway sees itself as a country that takes the rights of children more seriously than others’: Norwegian writer Magnus Nome The flipside of Norway’s often lauded “trust society” can manifest as a naive belief in the wisdom of its institutions, but there have long been discussions about Barnevernet, the child protection service: an imperfect system consisting of fallible humans, wielding the power to reach into the inner sanctum of the family. Systemic mistakes have been made: the European court of human rights ruled against Norway in multiple cases between 2018 and 2021. In a key case, the ECHR found the system in violation by not prioritising family reunification, treating an initial foster home placement as permanent from the start instead of working towards reunification with the biological mother. In another ruling against Barnevernet, the court criticised placing the son of a Muslim mother in an Evangelical Christian family, despite the mother’s request for her child to grow up in an environment reflecting his cultural and religious background. The former case resulted in a series of Norwegian supreme court rulings that made a reunification goal mandatory, ensured a higher level of minimum contact for parents and raised the threshold for forced adoption. The latter resulted in a revision in the country’s Child Welfare Act, mandating active steps to preserve a child’s cultural, religious and linguistic identity during foster placements. Fjord is a portrait of the system prior to these changes. A serious public debate about these issues has often been hard to accomplish, partly because discussion of specific cases is inevitably based on one-sided information, as Barnevernet adheres to strict confidentiality for the sake of the children involved. We only get the parents’ version, allowing them to form the public narrative, flipping the power dynamic. At the same time it relieves Barnevernet of having to counter concrete allegations of wrongdoing. There has long been a deep vein of harsh criticism directed at Barnevernet, reaching wide and far; social media groups numbering tens of thousands of furious members, more or less full-time activists (often with personal experience) and street protests in more than a dozen countries. It’s a surprising amount of international commotion around the social services of a small nation. View image in fullscreen Protests against Barnevernet in 2016. Photograph: CTK/Alamy Within the activist circles, the critiques frequently cross from principled concern into radical conspiracy theories: there are claims of adoptions for profit, organ harvesting and organised sex trade of minors, and accusations of being an ultraliberal indoctrination project, or a state-sanctioned eugenics programme. As a result, social workers have experienced harassment and threats. While the wild conspiracy theories have been debunked, most recently by the major newspaper VG, the reach of dramatic tales far surpasses that of well-documented refutations – not least when amplified by both foreign media with little local insight, and propaganda outlets such as the Russian RT, always happy to present “evidence” of the degeneracy of the liberal west. Such rampant misinformation ( not limited to Norway ) can at times hinder necessary debate, with criticism automatically assumed to originate from cranks. But most agree, including within Barnevernet itself, that an ongoing debate about the system is necessary and healthy. One can see Fjord, and the issue it portrays, as conservatism against liberal leftism, powerless individuals against an arrogant system, or a conflict between prioritising parents’ rights over those of the children. Most parents, myself among them, will insist they know what’s best for their own children better than any arm of the state – but some of those parents will also know of families with dangerously unfit parents that hold exactly the same opinion. Norway sees itself as a country that takes the rights of children more seriously than others, aware that while taking action carries the risk of harm, passive inaction and automatic acquiescence to parents can be equally damaging. Fjord may not be entirely objective or tell the complete story, but it’s a more nuanced work than the previous cinematic depiction of Barnevernet, Mrs Chatterjee vs Norway – a sensationalist Bollywood drama based on a mother’s account. To balance the film with a sympathetic portrayal of the dilemmas faced by social workers, the award-winning dramedy TV series Pernille, whose eponymous main character works in Barnevernet, is available on Netflix. Spain: minute of silence for train crash victims as king visits hospital Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 29 October 2026 - 23:47 GMT+1 Spain is mourning 69 people killed in a high-speed train collision near Toledo. As King Felipe VI visits a hospital treating the injured, rescuers continue searching the wreckage and a minute of silence is held at the crash site. … More Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo visited the scene, while King Felipe VI travelled to a hospital in Toledo treating survivors of the disaster. The monarch was greeted by hospital staff and other people waiting outside before entering the building. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Meanwhile, rescue teams continued searching the wreckage with sniffer dogs, as cranes lifted damaged carriages and emergency workers combed through debris scattered down a gravel embankment. One more body was recovered overnight, bringing the death toll to 69 , according to Castilla-La Mancha regional president Emiliano García-Page , who said 50 people remained in hospital . The collision occurred on Wednesday morning when a high-speed train operated by state-owned Renfe struck the rear of a stationary Iryo service in central Spain. At least three carriages were thrown down an embankment by the impact. The government declared three days of national mourning from Thursday, as the country's second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year raised fresh questions about railway safety. In January, 46 people were killed in another collision involving Renfe and Iryo trains on the same line. The latest crash, just four weeks before a national election , has also disrupted rail travel, with the high-speed route between Madrid and Seville closed and thousands of passengers seeking alternative transport.
